query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, controlled amount (around 1 atomic percent) of a carefully chosen doping element to a phosphorus-containing high‐entropy (or compositionally complex) alloy will improve its glass‐forming ability and enhance the thermal stability of its amorphous state by promoting enhanced local chemical ordering and increased topological connectivity that suppresses crystallization.
generation.material_initial_state: An amorphous phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy produced by melt-quenching (e.g., melt-spinning) with a well‐characterized baseline composition and processing history.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor (~1 at.%) addition of a doping element designed to modify local atomic arrangements (without presupposing its specific chemical class) into the alloy during the melting process.
generation.conditions: The alloy will be prepared by conventional melt-spinning under an inert atmosphere. Thermal stability will be tested using differential scanning calorimetry at a standard heating rate (e.g., 20 °C/min), and critical casting thickness will be measured to assess glass-forming ability. Microstructural characterization (via XRD and electron microscopy) is conducted at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced local chemical order and increased topological connectivity (i.e. a modified short-range atomic arrangement that reduces the number of favorable nucleation sites for crystallization).
generation.mechanism: The doping element is expected to alter the short-range order by increasing the diversity of local bonding environments. This change decreases atomic mobility, effectively elevating the energy barrier for crystallization and shifting the crystallization onset to higher temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped baseline, the doped alloy is predicted to exhibit both an increased critical casting thickness (indicative of improved glass-forming ability) and a higher onset temperature for crystallization in DSC measurements.
generation.baseline: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy manufactured by melt-spinning without the doping element, demonstrating a specific critical casting thickness and crystallization onset temperature.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to manifest under rapid quenching conditions typical of melt-spinning. It might not be apparent if processing conditions (e.g., significantly slower cooling rates) change, or in alloys with compositions substantially different from the baseline.
generation.uncertainty: The precise dopant identity and concentration required for optimal improvement are uncertain. Additionally, the magnitude of the enhancement in glass-forming ability and thermal stability may depend on the interaction between the dopant and the baseline alloy, necessitating empirical calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples with the same baseline alloy composition using melt-spinning: one set with the small (≈1 at.%) doping addition and another without. Characterize the amorphous structure using XRD and microscopy. Measure the DSC crystallization onset temperature at a fixed heating rate (e.g., 20 °C/min) and determine the critical casting thickness for both sets.
measurements: Critical casting thickness (indicator of glass-forming ability)
Microstructural confirmation of the amorphous state (via XRD and electron microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in both the DSC crystallization onset temperature and critical casting thickness relative to the undoped baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.
